title: Alan Smithee, the director who never was
hook: For 30 years, Hollywood's most prolific unhappy director did not exist.
peek: When a director felt a film had been taken out of their hands, the Directors Guild let them swap their name for Alan Smithee. The made-up director collected credits on films and TV for about three decades.
lede: Film directors in America are normally bound by guild rules to take their screen credit. But from the late 1960s, a director who could show the Directors Guild that a film had been recut or reshaped against their wishes could ask for a stand-in. The name on screen would read Alan Smithee, a director who never existed.

bullets.text: The name was first used on a 1969 western starring Richard Widmark. One director had been replaced by another partway through, and neither wanted the credit, so the guild invented someone who would.
The guild first thought of Al Smith, but that name was far too common. Smithee was unusual enough to stand out, which made it a quiet signal to anyone in the know.

A director had to make the case to a guild panel and, once approved, generally agreed not to talk publicly about why. Smithee also turned up on television cuts, such as the longer TV version of David Lynch's Dune.

The guild retired the name around 2000. A 1997 comedy about a director called Alan Smithee who wants to disown his film was itself disowned by its director, Arthur Hiller, and credited to Alan Smithee, which made the joke a little too public.
